video_title: Why the Pacific Northwest Coast is Insanely Empty
transcript: This is a population density map of the United States, showing where the roughly 340 million Americans who live across this country today are actually located. And if you pay attention to the coastlines, like almost everywhere else around the world, you'll notice a pretty familiar pattern. Most people in most parts of the country live pretty close by to them. Across the Northeast, you have the super densely populated coastal corridor between Boston, New York City, Philadelphia, Baltimore, and Washington, D.C., where more than 53 million people call home. Following the coast all the way down south around Florida and across the Gulf are cities like Charleston, Savannah, Jacksonville, Miami, Tampa, New Orleans, Houston, and even the rest of Texas. >> [music] >> The pattern of densely populated environments continues. Over on the opposite end of the country on the West Coast, most of California follows the same expected pattern. Going from the southern border with Mexico up to the San Francisco Bay, you'll find multiple major metropolises like San Diego, Los Angeles, and San Francisco that are collectively home to tens of millions of people. This is all pretty expected because, like everywhere else in the world, proximity to the coast and proximity to trade across the world's oceans and prosperity. But then, something really weird starts to happen to this familiar pattern when you look just a little further to the north past the San Francisco Bay and the Golden Gate that leads into it. From this point onwards, the heavily populated coastline of California abruptly comes to an end and it's replaced by the most sparsely populated long stretch of coastline found anywhere continental 48 United States. For nearly 700 miles of coastline, from just north of San Francisco through the rest of northern California, Oregon, and Washington up to the tip of the Olympic Peninsula, there are virtually no significant population centers at all. Across this whole vast length of coastline, there isn't even a single city at all that's home to any more than 30,000 residents. The biggest city, if you can even call it that, along this entire stretch of coastline for nearly 700 miles is Eureka [music] in northern California, which is only home to around 26,000 people. Besides for Eureka, there isn't even another town along this entire coast that's home to any more than 20,000 people. The biggest city on the Oregon coast, Coos Bay, has only 16,000 residents living there. While the biggest city on the Washington coast, Aberdeen, is home to only 17,000 people. Now, you might be thinking that this doesn't really make much sense, especially because both Oregon and Washington are home to some pretty big cities. Portland is home to a metropolitan area of roughly 2 and 1/2 million people, while the even larger Seattle-Tacoma metropolitan area is home to more than 4 million people. But the important thing to understand here is that neither Portland nor Seattle are actually located on the coastline of the open Pacific. Portland is located more than 70 miles away inland from the Pacific Ocean along the Willamette River near its confluence with the Columbia River. While Seattle is located on the protected inland waters of the Puget Sound, separated from the open ocean of the Pacific by the great Olympic Peninsula. So, both of these large metro areas are located well away from the coastal regions that I'm talking about here. And what's really astonishing is that nationwide, across the whole US, roughly 40% of the entire population lives within a coastal county somewhere that borders a major body of water. In Oregon, specifically, however, that ratio of the population that lives in coastal counties is only about 5% despite the state having more than 316 miles of coastline. In Washington, that ratio from the Columbia River in the south to the Olympic Peninsula in the north is even lower at only about 3% of the state population. This is, in my mind, a pretty extraordinary geographic anomaly because, as it is pretty much everywhere else, coastlines are normally some of the most economically valuable and heavily populated on the world. So, why then is this big old stretch of the US Pacific Northwest coast almost completely empty by comparison? Why did the millions of Americans who settled Oregon and Washington overwhelmingly choose to buck the greater trend >> [music] >> and chose to live inland instead of directly along the coast itself? And why did none of the seemingly promising coastal locations between San Francisco and the Olympic Peninsula ever develop into another major American city? To begin understanding all of this, the first thing we need to look at is the actual physical geography of the coastline itself and how it's impacted human population patterns for centuries. Because unlike the Atlantic and Gulf coast of the United States, which are covered by huge flat coastal plains that are easy to build on, or the area immediately around Los Angeles, the Pacific Northwest is dominated instead by mountains that run almost continuously right alongside of the ocean itself. Immediately to the north of San Francisco, the coast ranges of northern California extend all the way towards the Oregon border, where they're succeeded by the Oregon Coast Range, which continues all the way northward towards the Columbia River. And beyond that, the Willapa Hills and the Olympic Mountains dominate much of western Washington. Together, these mountain ranges form an almost continuous geographic barrier between the Pacific Ocean and the much flatter, more agriculturally productive interior valleys to the east. And while these coastal mountains aren't exactly gigantic to the ranges further to the east like the Cascades, Rockies, or Sierra Nevada, they're still big enough to restrict development to make infrastructure expensive and difficult to build through them. Across much of the coastline here, steep forested hills rise almost directly out of the ocean itself, leaving relatively little flat land available for large cities, extensive agriculture, or transportation infrastructure. And because of that, even when settlers were able to manage to establish communities along this coast, actually connecting those communities to one another or to the much more productive interior regions, was often both pretty difficult and pretty expensive. But the mountains here are really just the start of all the problems. The much, much bigger issue is that all across this region between San Francisco and the Olympic Peninsula, there is a truly remarkable dearth of usable natural harbors to use for trade and commerce. This is very, very unlike the East Coast of the US. Basically, everywhere over here on this side of the country, there are tons of natural harbors that have historically provided ships with sheltered places to dock and repair, load and unload cargo, and conduct trade with the outside world. Boston developed around an excellent harbor. New York City developed along one of the greatest natural harbors on the planet and at the mouth of the navigable Hudson River that connected into the fertile Hudson Valley. Philadelphia developed along the Delaware River that connected directly into the Delaware Bay. Baltimore and Washington D.C. developed around their access to the Chesapeake Bay, while Charleston and Savannah both developed along their own protected waterways and rivers as well. These locations were also useful beyond just their ability to serve as good harbors where ships could safely enter and leave. They were also connected to extensive networks of navigable rivers and relatively flat productive land that stretched deep into the interior, allowing goods and people to seamlessly move between the trade opportunity of the coastline and the market opportunities of the interior. The Atlantic and Gulf Coasts even [music] contain something that nowhere else in the world can match, the Intracoastal Waterway, a vast network of interconnected barrier islands, bays, rivers, sounds, and man-made canals that allow ships to travel for thousands of miles between Massachusetts and the US-Mexico border in Southern Texas, all through protected waters sheltered from the open ocean. There is nothing even remotely comparable to this geographic wonder that can be found over on the West Coast of the North American continent. Instead, especially along the Pacific Northwest, the coast is exposed directly to the violent swells of the Pacific with relatively few natural openings that provide safe access to protected waters. And the handful of bays and river mouths that actually do exist are frequently obstructed by dangerous sandbars, shallow channels, powerful currents, or mountainous terrain that makes transporting goods inland even more difficult on top of all of the coastal mountains. Southern California has excellent examples of natural harbors, like San Diego Bay and San Francisco Bay. San Francisco Bay, in particular, is a world-class natural harbor because it's huge and deep, contains a calm entrance from the open ocean through the Golden Gate, and is surrounded by extensive flat area suitable for settlement that can be reached through the navigable Sacramento and San Joaquin River systems. These rivers provide deep access from the San Francisco Bay into California's interior, including throughout the uber-fertile Central Valley for agricultural production and the mineral-rich Sierra Nevada mountains. When gold was discovered in the Sierra Nevada mountains of California in 1848, San Francisco was already geographically positioned to become the principal maritime gateway through which hundreds of thousands of ambitious gold seekers and their supplies could enter the region. Its favorable geography helped it transform it from a relatively small outpost before the Gold Rush into one of the most important cities on the entire Pacific coast afterwards. But then, when you travel north beyond the Golden Gate, all of these favorable geographic conditions begin to disappear from any other possible harbor site. >> [music] >> Indeed, there are actually a lot of bays along the coast in the Pacific Northwest that might initially seem capable of supporting major cities. But the more you look into them, the more it becomes apparent that they all have pretty serious nerves that are associated with them. One of the most interesting examples is Humboldt Bay, located about 270 mi north of San Francisco in northern California near the city of Eureka. At first glance, Humboldt Bay appears to be a location where another major Californian city should have been located. [music] It's the largest protected body of water along the Pacific coast anywhere between the San Francisco Bay and the Puget Sound with an extensive sheltered Bay behind a narrow entrance to the ocean. There's abundant rainfall and fresh water found all throughout the surrounding region and historically the near forest contains some of the largest and most valuable trees for the logging industry anywhere in the world. And yet, despite all of these apparent advantages, [music] Eureka still remains a city of only around 26,000 people today. The big problem is that Humboldt Bay's entrance from the Pacific is far less accommodating to ships than the sheltered waters inside of it might initially suggest. Ships approaching the Bay have historically needed to navigate a relatively narrow entrance that is plagued by shifting sandbars, powerful breakers, rough ocean swells, and frequently occurring fog. Once inside, the conditions get much calmer, but getting inside of it in the first place used to be extremely dangerous back in the day, especially before modern dredging and engineered jetties improved the harbor. And even after overcoming those problems, ships arriving at Humboldt Bay encountered another major obstacle that still persists to this day. The surrounding coast ranges effectively separate the harbor from California's economically productive interior, leaving relatively few practical transportation corridors through which goods could travel eastward or westward. Unlike San Francisco, which had access to the vast agricultural lands of the Central Valley and the mining regions of the Sierra Nevada, Humboldt Bay's natural economic hinterland was largely limited to the mountainous and heavily forested region that immediately surrounded it. This did make it a pretty good location for industries that could extract resources from the nearby forest and ship them away by sea, but a much less promising location for the kind of diversified commercial economy that could support a big city of hundreds of thousands or millions of people. But, for a while, though, the enormous forest that used to surround Humboldt Bay actually did create a pretty substantial economic boom back in the day. Northern California's coastal forests were once dominated by ancient coast redwoods, some of the tallest trees on the planet that can reach more than 100 m in height and survive for well over a thousand years. But, beginning in the 19th century, logging companies began harvesting these massive forests on an increasingly industrial scale. And Eureka became an important center for processing and exporting the valuable lumber. The industry expanded especially rapidly during and after the Second World War, when the introduction of more powerful machinery, trucks, bulldozers, and chainsaws made it possible to harvest the ancient forests at a speed that would have been unimaginable to the lumberjacks of the 19th century. And in the process of the lumber boom, Eureka actually did have a bit of a population boom, too. Between the end of the Second World War and the early 1960s, the population of Eureka expanded significantly from 17,000 people to more than 28,000 people. But, it's remained more or less stagnant ever since then. The ancient redwood forest were a finite resource. The faster that the logging companies harvested them, the more rapidly they depleted the very resource upon which the region's economy had grown dependent on. Today, only around 5% of the original old-growth coast redwood forest still remains, with the overwhelming majority having been logged and destroyed since European-American settlement began. And as the most accessible and valuable timber stands disappeared, the logging industry became increasingly constrained by resource depletion, environmental protections, and stiffer competition from other lumber-producing regions of the country. The number of jobs associated with the industry declined dramatically. And although Eureka and the surrounding communities never really disappeared, the region also never really managed to develop the kind of large, diversified economy that could sustain the rapid population growth those experienced elsewhere in central and southern California. And a very similar story to all of this unfolded a little further to the north along the coast of Oregon, too. Around another seemingly promising natural harbor called Coos Bay. Coos Bay is one of the most important natural harbors along the Oregon coast. And unlike many of the smaller estuaries that are found further to the north of it, it [music] actually does contain a substantial navigable channel that's capable of accommodating commercial shipping. In fact, the Port of Coos Bay describes itself as the largest coastal deep-draft harbor anywhere between San Francisco and the Puget Sound. And just like Humboldt Bay, the surrounding region historically contained huge amounts of valuable timber. But despite all of that, Coos Bay also suffered from basically the same geographic disadvantages as Humboldt Bay, too. Immediately inland from the coast are, of course, the mountains of the Oregon Coast Range, which separate the harbor from the much more agriculturally productive Willamette Valley to the east. The rivers feeding into Coos Bay are relatively small, and unlike the Hudson River for New York or the Sacramento River for San Francisco, they don't provide extensive navigable transportation corridors deep into the continent. This meant that Coos Bay could serve the regional timber-producing communities of southwestern Oregon, but it was poorly positioned to become the primary commercial gateway for the much larger and more economically valuable regions further inland. And these disadvantages became even more apparent during the later 19th century, [music] when the development of railroads began fundamentally transforming the American economy. Building railroads through the rugged mountains separating the coast from the interior was tremendously expensive. And the major railroad companies generally preferred to construct their lines through more favorable terrain and towards cities that already possess substantial commercial activity. Coos Bay did receive a small local railroad during the 1890s, but this line remained isolated from the broader national railroad network for another two decades longer. It wasn't all the way until 1916 that a railway finally connected the region directly to the Willamette Valley and the wider American rail system. And by that point, the major economic and population centers of the Pacific Northwest had already become firmly established elsewhere. >> [music] >> And this brings us to perhaps the most fascinating location along the entire Pacific Northwest coastline. Because unlike Humboldt Bay and Coos Bay, this next location actually does possess direct [music] access to an enormous river system stretching deep into the North American continent. In theory, it should have been one of the most geographically advantageous locations anywhere on the entire Pacific coast. And some of the earliest American settlers who arrived here genuinely believed that it was destined to become the site of one of the greatest cities in the entire United States. [music] That specific location was Astoria, Oregon, situated on a strategic peninsula near the mouth of the Columbia River. The Columbia River is one of the largest rivers on the North American continent, winding for roughly 1,200 miles from its headwaters in the Canadian Rocky Mountains through Washington and Oregon before finally emptying into the Pacific Ocean. Together with its various tributaries, including the massive Snake River, the Columbia drains an immense area of the Northwestern United States and Western Canada. It historically provided access to some of the most economically valuable agricultural lands and natural resources anywhere in the region. And right here, at the precise place where this mighty river finally reaches the ocean, sits the tiny little town of Astoria, which today is home to only around 10,000 people. But more than two centuries ago, Astoria was originally supposed to become something much, much bigger than this. In 1805, the famous Lewis and Clark expedition finally reached the mouth of the Columbia River after having traveled for thousands of miles across the then unexplored North American continent. And just a few years later after their arrival in 1811, the wealthiest man in America at the time, the Elon Musk of his age, John Jacob Astor, established a trading post near the mouth of the Columbia through his Pacific Fur Company, creating what would become the city of Astoria that bore his name. Astor's ambitions for the settlement at the time were colossal. He envisioned a vast commercial network connecting the interior of North America with Pacific Ocean and the lucrative markets of Asia, using the Columbia River as the principal transportation artery through which goods could travel between them. And geographically speaking, this actually seemed like a pretty reasonable idea because in many ways, the mouth of the Columbia River appears remarkably similar to the location of New York City over on the opposite side of the continent. New York developed around a huge natural harbor that connected to the Hudson River, which provided access to the fertile Hudson Valley and eventually, through the Erie Canal, to the Great Lakes and the vast interior of North America. Astoria, meanwhile, similarly sat at the mouth of an even larger river system that extended deeper into the northwestern interior. With access to the agricultural lands of the Willamette Valley, the Columbia Basin, and the valuable natural resources of the Rocky Mountains. So, on [music] paper, Astoria appeared to possess a lot of the same geographic advantages that had enabled New York to become America's greatest commercial city. And to many at the time, that meant that Astoria was destined to eventually become the New York City of the West Coast. But, as it turned out, there was a slight complication with these ambitious plans. While New York provided ships with a relatively safe and protected [music] entrance from the Atlantic Ocean, the mouth of the Columbia River is actually one of the most dangerous places for ships to navigate literally [music] anywhere on the planet Earth. You see, at the mouth of the Columbia, the huge volume of fresh water flowing through the river westward collides directly with the incoming tides, currents, and powerful ocean swells of the northern Pacific. [music] At the same time, the river also carries with it massive quantities of sediment downstream from the Rockies, which accumulate near its mouth as the water slows upon reaching the ocean. Over thousands of years, these processes created a very complicated system of shallow sandbars and shifting channels extending all across the entrance to the river. And because the sandbars are constantly being reshaped by waves, storms, and river currents, navigating through them could be extraordinarily difficult, especially for the sailing ships of the 18th and 19th centuries. During periods of bad weather, powerful ocean swells arriving from the west can collide with the river's outgoing current, producing steep, breaking waves that are exceptionally dangerous for ships attempting to cross the bar. And these conditions can become especially severe during the winter, when powerful storms sweep across the North Pacific and send powerful waves crashing towards the coastline. And even when the weather appears to be relatively calm, rapidly changing and unpredictable currents, submerged sandbars, and poor visibility can all combine to create serious hazards for ships who are unfamiliar with the entrance. In fact, the mouth of the Columbia River was so difficult for early European explorers to identify and navigate that several expeditions just sailed right past it without even successfully entering it at all. In 1788, the British explorer John Meares attempted to locate the river's entrance, but failed to recognize a navigable passage, and subsequently gave the nearby headland to the rather pessimistic name of Cape Disappointment. It wasn't until 1792 that the American Captain Robert Gray successfully crossed the bar and actually entered into the Columbia River aboard his ship, the USS Columbia Rediviva, which established the river's name in the process. [music] And the danger of this entrance became increasingly apparent as more ships began attempting to cross it. Throughout the 19th century, vessels were repeatedly driven onto sandbars, smashed apart by breaking waves, or wrecked along the nearby coastline during storms and periods of poor visibility. The mouth of the Columbia eventually acquired a reputation as being one of the most dangerous maritime passages in the United States, becoming the most notorious part of a much larger region that eventually became known as the graveyard of the Pacific, where thousands of ships have been recorded to have been wrecked all across since the late 18th century. The danger wasn't just theoretical, either. In January of 1852, the steamship General Warren was attempting to leave the Columbia River on a voyage toward San Francisco when it encountered severe conditions near the bar. The vessel became stranded and began breaking apart in the surf, and despite efforts to obtain assistance from nearby Astoria, more than 30 passengers and crew members on board ultimately lost their lives in the disaster. It became one of the most infamous early shipwrecks in the region and helped demonstrate just how dangerous maritime commerce through the Columbia River entrance could be. Over the following few decades, the US government invested massive resources into improving the entrance, constructing huge jetties to stabilize the navigation channel, and undertaking extensive dredging operations to maintain sufficient depth for commercial vessels. These engineering projects substantially improved the reliability of navigation through the river mouths, but they couldn't completely eliminate the underlying natural forces responsible for making the Columbia bar so dangerous in the first place. Even today, despite modern ships, radar, satellite navigation, weather forecasting, and more than a century of engineering improvements, the Columbia River bar remains a highly challenging maritime passage. Large commercial vessels entering and leaving the river routinely depend on specially trained maritime pilots who possess extensive knowledge of the constantly changing conditions at the entrance. The Columbia River bar pilots are among the most highly specialized maritime professionals in America, and their job is considered to be sufficiently dangerous and demanding enough that they receive exceptionally high compensation for their services, sometimes to the tune of $500,000 a year in annual salary today. The nearby US Coast Guard Station at Cape Disappointment even hosts the National Motor Lifeboat School, where rescue crews are trained to operate in some of the most difficult surf conditions encountered anywhere in American waters. But here's the really interesting thing about all of this. Despite all of the dangers associated with crossing the Columbia River bar, the river itself still offered such valuable access to the interior that maritime callers through its entrance just continued expanding. Ships were willing to accept the risks of crossing the bar because the Columbia provided access to a large and increasingly productive economic region. The problem for Astoria was that once ships had successfully crossed the dangerous entrance, there wasn't necessarily any reason for them to stop at Astoria itself. Because only about 100 miles further upstream, along the Columbia and Willamette Rivers, there was another location that possessed several natural advantages over Astoria. And that location would eventually become the largest city in Oregon, Portland. Portland was established during the 1840s along the Willamette River, not that far upstream from where the Willamette joins the Columbia. And unlike Astoria, which was located along a relatively narrow strip of coastal land surrounded by steep forested hills, Portland occupied a position immediately adjacent to the vast and fertile Willamette Valley. This valley stretches southward for more than 100 miles through western Oregon and contains some of the most productive agricultural land found anywhere in the Pacific Northwest. It was precisely this valley that attracted huge numbers of American settlers traveling westward along the Oregon Trail during the 19th century. And while Astoria occupied the entrance to the Columbia River, Portland was located much closer to the actual farms, mills, forests, and growing communities that would produce the goods that were actually being transported along it. Agricultural products could be moved northward along the Willamette River to Portland, where they could then be loaded up on the larger ships for transport down the Columbia and out into the Pacific. And meanwhile, goods arriving from overseas could just be unloaded in Portland and then distributed all throughout the Willamette Valley and the growing settlements of the interior there, far easier than if they had unloaded at Astoria. All of this gave Portland a substantial advantage over Astoria. A ship arriving from San Francisco or another Pacific port already needed to cross the dangerous Columbia River bar regardless of which city it intended to visit. [music] And once it had successfully entered the river, continuing upstream toward Portland brought the ship all that much closer to the region's principal agricultural markets and commercial customers. Astoria was located at the gateway, [music] but Portland was located closer to all of the economic activity that made that gateway valuable in the first place. And then, the arrival of the railroads made the geographic divide between the two cities even more significant. Portland was connected to the transcontinental railroad network in 1883, securing its position as one of the principal commercial gateways between the Pacific Northwest and the rest of the US. Astoria, by contrast, was repeatedly bypassed by proposed railroad projects, and it didn't finally receive a direct rail connection to the broader network until 1898, 15 years after Portland did. By the time that connection arrived, Portland had already enjoyed decades of economic advantages that Astoria struggled to ever overcome. Astoria also experienced several devastating fires, including a particularly destructive downtown fire in 1922, which destroyed much of the city's commercial district. Its local economy remained heavily dependent on industries like fishing, salmon canning, lumber, and maritime trade, all of which were vulnerable to changing resource supplies and market conditions. Those industries were enough to support a prosperous regional community, but they never generated the kind of diversified economy that could have transformed Astoria into the great Pacific metropolis that its early promoters had initially imagined. And so, despite being established decades before Portland was, despite possessing direct access to the mouth of one of North America's largest river systems, and despite once being envisioned as a major commercial gateway between America and Asia, Astoria always remained a relatively small city. Portland, meanwhile, grew into a major metropolitan area. The overwhelming majority of Oregon's population eventually became concentrated along the inland Willamette Valley corridor, stretching southward through Salem and Eugene. And this is ultimately why the population distribution of the Pacific Northwest developed in such an unusual way. The region's largest cities didn't grow directly along the open Pacific coastline, because the most economically favorable locations were instead found further inland, either along the fertile Willamette Valley or around the sheltered waters of the Puget Sound, where Seattle and Tacoma eventually coalesced around. Meanwhile, the exposed coastline was left with smaller communities that depended heavily upon industries like logging, fishing, and eventually tourism. And while the Pacific Northwest coastline is extraordinarily beautiful, it's also not particularly well suited for the same kind of beach tourism that helped transform places like Southern California and Florida into big population centers later in the 20th century. The cold California current that drags frigid water south from the Arctic and Alaska keeps ocean temperatures off of the coast here relatively chilly throughout the whole year. While powerful waves, dangerous rip currents, frequent fog, and heavy winter rainfall all make the coastline a lot less appealing for traditional beach recreation as well. Astoria and Cannon Beach on the coast receive annual rainfall rates of 70 and 90 in per year respectively. While Portland, just 70 mi away further inland, only receives about 37 in per year, about half of the total of the coast. The difference in Washington is even more stark [music] where parts of the Olympic Peninsula receive about 120 in of rainfall per year compared to Seattle that only gets about 39 in per year, only about a third of what the Olympic Peninsula gets despite Seattle's very rainy reputation. A lot of people just don't want to deal with that much rainfall throughout the year on the coast. And then, there's another final factor that makes the Pacific Northwest coastline even more unusual and potentially much more dangerous than almost any other coastline, not just in the United States, but anywhere in the world. And unlike the dangerous harbors, mountainous terrain, cold ocean waters, and high rainfall, this particular geographic disadvantage wasn't fully understood by modern scientists until relatively recently. Because directly offshore of Northern California, Oregon, and Washington lies the roughly 700 mile long Cascadia Subduction [music] Zone, where the oceanic Juan de Fuca tectonic plate and its neighboring fragments are slowly being forced beneath the North American plate. As these plates become locked together, colossal quantities of stress slowly accumulate over a period of centuries before eventually being released in catastrophic mega thrust earthquakes that can approach a magnitude of 9.0. These earthquakes are powerful enough to violently shake much of the Pacific Northwest, while simultaneously displacing enormous volumes of seawater and generating devastating tsunamis that can reach the nearby coastline within minutes. And what's especially terrifying about this is that scientists only began fully appreciating the scale of the danger during the late 20th century after discovering evidence of ancient tsunamis, submerged forests, and sudden coastal subsidence throughout the region. By combining all of this geological evidence with historical records from Japan that described a mysterious tsunami that struck the eastern Japanese coastline in January of 1700, researchers eventually determined that one of these magnitude 9.0 earthquakes had occurred along the Cascadia Subduction Zone on January 26th of 1700. The resulting tsunami devastated portions of the Pacific Northwest coastline before also traveling thousands of miles across the Pacific Ocean to hit Japan, too. [music] Indigenous communities also preserved oral histories describing catastrophic earthquakes and flooding along the coast. And importantly, geological records indicate that these devastating earthquakes and tsunamis have happened repeatedly over thousands of years, meaning that another one will eventually occur again here, too. According to a 2025 assessment by the US Geological Survey, there is approximately a 10% to 15% chance of another magnitude 9.0 earthquake rocking the Cascadia subduction zone sometime within the next 50 years. While the probability of a smaller magnitude 8.0 earthquake in the southern portions of the fault, located off northern California and southern Oregon, is estimated to be at around 30% in the next 50 years. Nobody knows precisely when the next disaster will happen because the intervals between past earthquakes have varied considerably. It could happen tomorrow, or it could still remain centuries away in the distant future. But whenever it does eventually and inevitably happen, the consequences for many coastal communities in the Pacific Northwest could be catastrophic. With powerful shaking, destroyed infrastructure, and gigantic tsunamis potentially reaching some low-lying communities within only minutes after the shaking stops. And while this lurking danger doesn't explain why major cities failed to develop along the ghost line during the 19th century, since the threat wasn't widely understood at the time, it certainly creates yet another major obstacle to extensive future development here, particularly in vulnerable low-lying areas exposed to potential tsunamis. And so, when you put all of these factors together, the extraordinary emptiness of the American Pacific Northwest coastline begins to make a lot more sense. Its rugged mountains, its few and dangerous harbors, limited transportation connections, and lack of extensive navigable rivers historically pushed the region's economic development further inland, toward Portland and the Willamette Valley, and toward Seattle and the protected waters of the Puget Sound. And once those cities had already become established, their economic gravity continued attracting the population and investments and railroads that the exposed coastline struggled to ever compete for. Combined with its cold waters, challenging weather, limited industries, and the now well-known ever-present geological threat of the Cascadia subduction zone affecting local anxieties, it's unlikely that this vast stretch of coastline will ever actually develop into anything resembling the heavily populated coast of Southern California or the Eastern [music] United States. But, seen in another way, that's also part of what makes this whole region so exceptional, too. Because the same geographic obstacles that have historically prevented major cities from developing here have also helped preserve some of the most spectacular and relatively untouched coastal landscapes remaining anywhere in the continental United States today. And that's likely to remain part of its appeal to some of us for a very long time to come. And speaking about seemingly small differences in geography can end up having enormous consequences.
